rv.q: David Adjmi's superb, gorgeously textured drama — which scooped a hatful of Tony Awards after its first New York run and is brilliantly staged here by Daniel Aukin and an outstanding cast — sinks us into the creative fever dream that follows.
The show captures the sleepless grind and tedium of recording but also the euphoria when the sound comes together.
In between the kit-tinkering and longueurs are moments of creative transcendence, including a late-night epiphany so electrifying that the sound waves will excite your internal organs.
Stereophonic carries it off spectacularly well.
Daniel Aukin’s production feels rich and sumptuous enough to be forgiven.
But in electing to give us a piece that dwells on the painful, mundane minutiae, Adjmi is authentic almost to a fault.
It's all very cool, but is this play chart-topping material? I don't think so.
Even if the denouement doesn't quite deliver, Stereophonic is effortlessly cool. We're not worthy.
Stereophonic arrives on the London stage with the resonance of a guitar classic.
Like the musicians labouring long hours in the studio, the director Daniel Aukin has reportedly spent 11 years working on this production: it was 11 years well spent.

STEREOPHONIC has landed in London after much hype and excitement on Broadway where it garnered 13 Tony nominations during awards season — more than any other play in the award’s history. It went on to win in 5 categories, perhaps most importantly for Best Play.
Stereophonic is an endlessly rich, deeply human labour of love.
There is no doubt that the West End premiere of Stereophonic is going to be one huge hit.
Like any great record, Stereophonic feels like one that will grow and grow with repeated playback.
Daniel Aukin's immersive production is impressively authentic – right down to Enver Chakartash's costumes – though the pace, and our concentration, inevitably dips.
Daring direction from Daniel Aukin allows for electric anticipation, and means our attention is maintained across the three-hour runtime.

In its long stretches of extraneous ennui, Stereophonic risks undoing what, when it is at full power, it succeeds in doing: acknowledging that the messiest of behind-the-scenes chaos can, just sometimes, produce sheer musical magic.
Despite its pedigree and moments of brilliance, this production at the Duke of York’s Theatre doesn’t quite hit all the right notes.
Coming up with the right themes but striving to stay in tune with its audience, Stereophonic sets up an interesting track for an enthralling narrative to unravel.

cn.t: A meticulously crafted, immersive dive into a 1970s rock band's fraught recording process earns widespread praise for its authenticity and performances, though some critics find its three-hour runtime indulgent and slow-paced.
